name: Learn: Cluster Hardening (hardened)
objective: CKS › Cluster + System Hardening (15% + 15%). Drill EVERY hardening corner harder than the exam on a real multi-node kind cluster: control-plane manifest perms, kubelet read-only port + anonymous-auth + authz mode, two apiserver admission/flag hardenings, least-privilege RBAC, ServiceAccount token hardening, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.
description: Eight strict node-level practicals on a real multi-node cluster via docker exec ($CP control-plane, $W1/$W2 workers). Each Check shows which requirements you met and the exact reason for any you missed.

questions.title: Harden control-plane manifest file permissions
questions.teach:
Static pod manifests under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` carry sensitive flags, so CIS wants them mode `0600` (`rw-------`) and owned `root:root`. On a kind cluster each node is a container, so operate via `docker exec $CP ...` and verify with `stat -c '%a %U:%G'`.

**Gotcha:** changing a manifest's mode/owner does NOT restart its pod (safe live) — only editing its *contents* does.
questions.prompt:
The kube-scheduler static pod manifest on control-plane `$CP` was left world/group readable at mode `644`. Set `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` to exactly mode `600`, owned `root:root`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` prints `600 root:root`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root

questions.title: Disable the kubelet read-only port
questions.teach:
The kubelet **read-only port** (`10255`) serves pod/node metadata with no auth and no TLS. CIS requires it off: set `readOnlyPort: 0` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `systemctl restart kubelet`. Any non-zero value leaves it enabled.

**Gotcha:** the edit does nothing until the kubelet restarts, and the node goes `NotReady` briefly — wait ~20s and confirm it's `Ready` again.
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W1` the kubelet is serving its read-only port (seeded as `readOnlyPort: 10255`). Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W1` so `readOnlyPort: 0`, then restart the kubelet and give the node ~20s to report `Ready` again.

Target: the config on `$W1` has `readOnlyPort: 0` AND node `$W1` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: node $W1 is still Ready after the kubelet restart

questions.title: Lock down kubelet authn/authz
questions.teach:
An unprotected kubelet lets anyone hit its API. CIS requires `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false` and `authorization.mode: Webhook` (not blanket `AlwaysAllow`) in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then a kubelet restart.

**Gotcha:** `anonymous.enabled` is nested under `authentication:` and `mode` under `authorization:` — edit the right blocks, not stray top-level keys.
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W2` the kubelet was seeded insecure: `authentication.anonymous.enabled: true` and `authorization.mode: AlwaysAllow`. Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W2` so anonymous auth is **disabled** and the authorization mode is **Webhook**, then restart the kubelet and let `$W2` go `Ready` again.

Target: on `$W2`, `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false` AND `authorization.mode: Webhook`, and node `$W2` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: In `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W2`, set the `enabled:` under `authentication.anonymous` to `false` and the `mode:` under `authorization` to `Webhook`; then `docker exec $W2 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W2 sed -i 's/^\(\s*enabled:\).*/\1 false/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # under authentication.anonymous
docker exec $W2 sed -i 's/^\(\s*mode:\).*/\1 Webhook/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml       # under authorization
docker exec $W2 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W2   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: kubelet on $W2: anonymous auth false + authorization mode Webhook, node Ready

questions.title: Re-enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin
questions.teach:
`NodeRestriction` is an apiserver **admission controller** limiting each kubelet to modifying only its own Node and the Pods bound to it. Enable it in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` via `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...` — one flag, comma-separated.

**Gotcha:** saving the manifest auto-restarts the apiserver; a typo takes it DOWN — wait ~20–60s for it to come back.
questions.prompt:
Setup removed `NodeRestriction` from the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins`. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP` so the flag includes `NodeRestriction` again (keep any other plugins), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `NodeRestriction` in `--enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $CP sed -i '/- kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` (or append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value). Wait ~20s for the restart.
questions.solution:
# Setup removed the flag line, so add it back under the kube-apiserver args:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# (If the flag already exists with other plugins, instead append ,NodeRestriction to its value.)
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins

questions.title: Turn off apiserver profiling
questions.teach:
The apiserver's `/debug/pprof` profiling endpoints leak internals, so CIS wants `--profiling=false` on the kube-apiserver. Add it to `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP`; saving restarts the apiserver.

**Gotcha:** `--profiling` defaults to `true`, so merely omitting the flag is NOT compliant — it must be present and set to `false`.
questions.prompt:
Harden the kube-apiserver on `$CP` by adding `--profiling=false` to its static pod manifest (`/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml`), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `--profiling=false` in its command args.
questions.hint: `docker exec $CP sed -i '/- kube-apiserver$/a\    - --profiling=false' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml`, then wait ~20s and check `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep profiling`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --profiling=false' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart, then:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep -- --profiling

questions.title: Least-privilege RBAC for a workload
questions.teach:
Give a workload the minimum API access: a narrow namespaced **Role** (only the verbs/resources needed) bound to its ServiceAccount via a **RoleBinding** — never `cluster-admin`. Imperatively: `kubectl create role r --verb=get,list --resource=pods` then `kubectl create rolebinding rb --role=r --serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>`.

**Gotcha:** `--serviceaccount` takes `ns:name`, not just the name.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn` a ServiceAccount `reader` already exists. Create a Role granting only `get,list` on `pods` and a RoleBinding binding it to that SA.

Target: SA `reader` can `list pods` (`yes`) but cannot `delete pods` (`no`) in `cks-learn`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods`, then `kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n cks-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl -n cks-learn create rolebinding reader-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=cks-learn:reader
kubectl auth can-i list pods   --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:reader -n cks-learn   # no

verification.description: SA reader can list pods but cannot delete pods in cks-learn

questions.title: ServiceAccount token hardening
questions.teach:
By default every pod auto-mounts a ServiceAccount token an attacker could steal. For pods that never call the API, set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the **ServiceAccount**, then point the pod at it with `serviceAccountName` so it gets no token volume.

**Gotcha:** `automountServiceAccountToken` sits at the **top level** of the SA object, not inside a `spec:` block — a common YAML mistake.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-learn`, create a ServiceAccount `no-token` with `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, then run a pod `hardened` (image `busybox:1.36`, e.g. `sleep 3600`) using that ServiceAccount.

Target: SA `no-token` has `automountServiceAccountToken: false` AND pod `hardened` runs as SA `no-token` with no SA token volume mounted.
questions.hint: Create the SA with `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (top level), then create the pod with `serviceAccountName: no-token`. Apply with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-token
  namespace: cks-learn
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened
  namespace: cks-learn
spec:
  serviceAccountName: no-token
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML

verification.description: SA no-token has automount disabled and pod hardened uses it with no token mounted

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: RBAC that grants the wrong access
questions.teach:
When `kubectl auth can-i` says `no` for something a SA should have, the fault is usually a wrong `resources`, `verbs`, or `apiGroups` entry in the **Role**. Inspect with `kubectl -n cks-learn get role <r> -o yaml` and compare each rule to what's required.

**Gotcha:** fix the existing Role, don't create a second one — and keep it least-privilege: grant exactly what's needed, nothing more.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-learn`, SA `audit-sa` is bound (via RoleBinding `audit-rb` → Role `audit-role`) but it still **cannot** `list pods` — the Role was seeded pointing at the wrong resource. Diagnose and fix the Role so `audit-sa` can `get,list` pods, without granting write access. Don't delete and rebuild from scratch — find and fix what's wrong.

Target: SA `audit-sa` can `list pods` (`yes`) but cannot `delete pods` (`no`) in `cks-learn`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-learn get role audit-role -o yaml` — its rule lists the wrong `resources` (not `pods`). `kubectl -n cks-learn edit role audit-role` and set `resources: ["pods"]` with `verbs: ["get","list"]`.
questions.solution:
# describe/get shows audit-role grants get,list on 'services' instead of 'pods'
kubectl -n cks-learn patch role audit-role --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/rules/0/resources","value":["pods"]}]'
kubectl auth can-i list pods   --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:audit-sa -n cks-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:cks-learn:audit-sa -n cks-learn   # no

verification.description: SA audit-sa can list pods but cannot delete pods in cks-learn (Role fault fixed)
